note: Written tasks (proofs, constructions, graph sketches, drawings and explanations): never marked automatically. An educator marks each answer against the rubric (written@1); a drawn answer uses the drawing pad (draw@1). "serves" names the curriculum outcomes a task assesses. Original, written for OpenPath; CC0; provisional until educator-reviewed.

tasks.prompt: Prove that √2 is irrational. Write each step of your argument and say why it follows.

rubric.criterion: Assumes the opposite: √2 = a/b with a, b whole numbers with no common factor (b ≠ 0)
Squares to get a² = 2b² and concludes a² is even, so a is even
Writes a = 2c, gets b² = 2c², so b is even
States the contradiction (a and b share the factor 2) and concludes √2 is irrational

tasks.guidance: A complete proof by contradiction has all four steps. Accept any correct equivalent argument (e.g. via prime factorisation and the parity of exponents). Award a step only if its reason is given, not just the equation.

tasks.prompt: Prove that √3 is irrational. Give the reason for each step.

rubric.criterion: Assumes √3 = a/b in lowest terms
Shows 3 divides a² and so 3 divides a (because 3 is prime)
Writes a = 3c and shows 3 divides b
Concludes from the contradiction

tasks.guidance: The key reason is that if a prime p divides a², then p divides a. Accept equivalent arguments.

tasks.prompt: Given that √5 is irrational, prove that 3 + 2√5 is irrational. Give the reason for each step.

rubric.criterion: Assumes 3 + 2√5 = r is rational
Rearranges to √5 = (r − 3)/2
Explains that (r − 3)/2 is rational, contradicting that √5 is irrational

tasks.guidance: The rearranged expression must be argued rational (rationals are closed under subtraction and division by a non-zero rational).

tasks.prompt: Using only a ruler and compasses, construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment AB that is 7 cm long. Say why the line you draw is perpendicular to AB and passes through its midpoint. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws arcs from A and from B with the same radius, more than half of AB
Joins the two points where the arcs meet
Explains why: each intersection point is the same distance from A and B (equal radii), and the set of such points is the perpendicular bisector

tasks.guidance: If the learner uploads or describes a drawing, check that the radius is more than half of AB. A full reason refers to equal distances (or to congruent triangles). Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Using only a ruler and compasses, bisect an angle of 70°. Explain why the two angles you make are equal. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws an arc from the vertex cutting both arms
From the two cut points draws equal arcs that meet inside the angle
Joins the vertex to the meeting point
Explains the equal angles by congruent triangles (SSS)

tasks.guidance: Accept any correct ruler-and-compass method. The reason must name congruent triangles or equal distances. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: With a ruler and compasses only (no protractor), construct an angle of 60°. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws a ray and an arc from its starting point
Uses the same radius from where the arc cuts the ray, to cut the first arc
Joins the start to the new point to make the 60° angle

tasks.guidance: The construction makes an equilateral triangle; an explanation is not required at Grade 6 but may be credited in feedback. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Divide a line segment AB of length 8 cm in the ratio 3 : 2 using a ruler and compasses, and explain why the point you find divides AB in that ratio. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws a ray at an acute angle from one end and marks 5 equal steps
Joins the 5th mark to the other end of the segment
Draws a parallel through the 3rd mark to meet the segment
Explains by the Basic Proportionality Theorem (or similar triangles)

tasks.guidance: Equal steps must be marked with the compasses at a fixed radius. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct a quadrilateral PQRS with PQ = 5 cm, QR = 4 cm, RS = 6 cm, PS = 5.5 cm and diagonal PR = 7 cm. Say why these five measurements are enough. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Constructs triangle PQR from PQ, QR and PR
Constructs triangle PRS on the other side of PR from RS and PS
Explains that the diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles, each fixed by three sides

tasks.guidance: Two triangles sharing the diagonal; check the second triangle is on the opposite side of PR. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Locate √5 on the number line using a ruler and compasses, and explain why the point you mark is √5 units from 0. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Builds a right triangle with legs 2 and 1 at the origin (or equivalent)
Uses Pythagoras: the hypotenuse is √(2² + 1²) = √5
Draws an arc centred at 0 with the hypotenuse as radius to meet the number line

tasks.guidance: Any right triangle with legs whose squares sum to 5 is fine. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Prove by mathematical induction that 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 for every positive whole number n.

rubric.criterion: Checks the base case n = 1
States the induction hypothesis for n = k
Shows the statement for n = k + 1 using the hypothesis, with correct algebra
Concludes by the principle of induction

tasks.guidance: The step must use the hypothesis explicitly: add (k + 1) to k(k + 1)/2 and simplify to (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.

tasks.prompt: Prove by mathematical induction that 3ⁿ − 1 is divisible by 2 for every positive whole number n.

rubric.criterion: Base case: 3 − 1 = 2
Assumes 3ᵏ − 1 = 2m
Concludes by induction

tasks.guidance: Accept any correct rearrangement in the step.

tasks.prompt: Two players take turns to say 1, 2 or 3 numbers counting up from 1 (the first player may say "1", or "1, 2", or "1, 2, 3"). Whoever says 21 wins. Would you rather go first or second? Explain a strategy that always wins.

rubric.criterion: Finds the safe numbers 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21 (one more than multiples of 4)
Explains always making the total said in a round 4 (answer the opponent’s 1, 2 or 3 with 3, 2 or 1)
Chooses to go first (say "1") and explains why

tasks.guidance: The winning positions are 1 more than multiples of 4; the first player says 1 and then keeps each round to 4 numbers.

tasks.prompt: Draw a line l and mark a point P that is 4 cm away from it. Using a ruler and compasses, construct the line through P that is parallel to l, and say how you know the two lines are parallel. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Constructs a perpendicular from P to l (arc from P cutting l twice, then equal arcs from those two points), meeting l at M
Constructs a second perpendicular, to PM at the point P
Explains that both lines are perpendicular to PM, so they never meet: they are parallel

tasks.guidance: Any correct ruler-and-compass method is fine (e.g. copying an angle to make equal corresponding angles). The reason must connect the steps to parallel lines (two lines perpendicular to the same line, or equal corresponding/alternate angles). Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Draw a triangle ABC in which the angle at B is acute and BC is the longest side. Construct the altitude from A to BC (the line from A that meets BC at a right angle). Say why your line meets BC at a right angle. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws an arc centred at A that cuts BC (extended if needed) at two points X and Y
From X and Y, with the same radius, draws arcs that cross on the side of BC away from A
Joins A to the crossing point; the altitude is the part from A to BC
Explains that A and the crossing point are each the same distance from X and Y, so the line is perpendicular to XY (that is, to BC)

tasks.guidance: This is the perpendicular from a point to a line, used in a triangle. Credit 'extend BC if needed'. The reason may be given as equal distances from X and Y. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct a rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 3.5 cm, using a ruler and compasses (no protractor or set square). Say how you know each corner is a right angle. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws AB = 7 cm, measuring it with the compasses from the ruler
Constructs a perpendicular to AB at B (and/or at A) with ruler and compasses
Marks BC = 3.5 cm on the perpendicular and finds D (arcs of 3.5 cm from A and 7 cm from C, or a second perpendicular at A)
Explains the right angles: constructed at B (and A), and opposite sides are equal, so the shape is a rectangle

tasks.guidance: At Grade 6, 'I constructed the right angles at A and B and made AD = BC = 3.5 cm' is a full reason. A shape with the right side lengths but no constructed right angle is not yet a rectangle. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct triangle LMN with LM = 7 cm, MN = 6 cm and LN = 5 cm. First check that a triangle with these sides exists, then construct it, and explain why the point N you find is the right one. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Checks the triangle inequality (for example 5 + 6 > 7)
Draws one side, e.g. LM = 7 cm
Draws an arc of radius 5 cm centred at L and an arc of radius 6 cm centred at M, meeting at N
Explains that N is on both arcs, so LN = 5 cm and MN = 6 cm

tasks.guidance: Any side may be the base, as long as the arcs use the matching radii from the matching ends. The check may be written as 'the two shorter sides add to more than the longest'. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, angle A = 60° and AC = 4.5 cm. (You may make the 60° angle with compasses, or with a protractor if you have one.) Say why these three measurements fix exactly one triangle. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws AB = 6 cm
Makes the 60° angle at A (compass method or protractor)
Marks AC = 4.5 cm along the arm of the angle and joins C to B
Explains that the angle is between the two given sides (SAS), so C has only one possible place

tasks.guidance: The angle must be at A, between AB and AC. Credit either way of making 60°. 'Only one place for C' or 'SAS fixes the triangle' are both full reasons. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct triangle PQR with PQ = 6.5 cm, angle P = 40° and angle Q = 110° (a protractor may be used for the angles). Then explain why there is NO triangle with PQ = 6.5 cm, angle P = 80° and angle Q = 110°. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws PQ = 6.5 cm
Makes 40° at P and 110° at Q on the same side of PQ
Takes R where the two arms meet
Explains that 80° + 110° = 190° is more than 180°, so the arms do not meet on that side (the angles of a triangle add to 180°)

tasks.guidance: The two angles must be drawn on the same side of PQ. For the second part, 'the arms would only meet if the two angles added to less than 180°' is a full reason. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct a right-angled triangle XYZ with the right angle at Y, XY = 6 cm and hypotenuse XZ = 10 cm, using a ruler and compasses. Explain each step. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws XY = 6 cm
Constructs the perpendicular to XY at Y
Draws an arc of radius 10 cm centred at X to cut the perpendicular at Z
Explains why: the right angle is at Y and Z is 10 cm from X, so XZ is the hypotenuse (RHS)

tasks.guidance: The arc must be centred at X (the other end of the hypotenuse), not at Y. The learner may note YZ = 8 cm by Pythagoras; credit it in feedback. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Prove that when you multiply any two odd numbers, the answer is odd. Checking examples is not enough: your argument must work for every pair of odd numbers.

rubric.criterion: Writes the two odd numbers as 2m + 1 and 2n + 1 with different letters for whole numbers m and n
Multiplies correctly: (2m + 1)(2n + 1) = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1
Rewrites it as 2(2mn + m + n) + 1
Concludes that this is one more than a multiple of 2, so it is odd, for every m and n

tasks.guidance: Using the same letter for both numbers (2n + 1 squared) proves only that the square of an odd number is odd: award at most the last two criteria. Examples alone earn nothing, but may be praised in feedback as a good first check.

tasks.prompt: A number trick: think of a number, add 3, multiply by 4, subtract 8, divide by 4, then subtract the number you first thought of. Everyone ends with 1. Use algebra to explain why this always happens.

rubric.criterion: Lets the starting number be a letter, e.g. n
Writes each step correctly: n + 3, 4n + 12, 4n + 4, n + 1
Shows that subtracting n leaves 1 whatever n is, and says that this is why it always works

tasks.guidance: Brackets may be expanded at any stage, e.g. 4(n + 3) − 8 = 4n + 4. An explanation using a 'bag of counters' picture is fine if it matches the algebra.

tasks.prompt: Take any two-digit number, reverse its digits, and add the two numbers (for example 47 + 74 = 121). Prove that the answer is always a multiple of 11.

rubric.criterion: Writes the number as 10a + b, with digits a and b, and its reversal as 10b + a
Adds to get 11a + 11b
Writes 11a + 11b = 11(a + b)
Concludes it is a multiple of 11 for every choice of digits

tasks.guidance: Writing 'ab' for the number is a common slip (it means a × b); credit only if the learner makes clear it means 10a + b.

tasks.prompt: ABCD is a parallelogram (AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC). The diagonal AC is drawn. Prove that triangles ABC and CDA are congruent, and so AB = CD. Give a reason for every statement.

rubric.criterion: ∠BAC = ∠DCA, because they are alternate angles (AB ∥ DC)
∠BCA = ∠DAC, because they are alternate angles (AD ∥ BC)
AC = CA (common side)
Concludes △ABC ≅ △CDA by ASA, and AB = CD as corresponding parts

tasks.guidance: Check that the angles are paired with the correct parallel lines and that the vertices of the triangles are matched in order (A↔C, B↔D, C↔A).

tasks.prompt: In △ABC, ∠B = ∠C. Prove that AB = AC. Write the proof with a reason for every statement (you may draw the bisector of ∠A).

rubric.criterion: Draws AD bisecting ∠A, meeting BC at D
In △ABD and △ACD: ∠B = ∠C (given), ∠BAD = ∠CAD (construction), AD = AD (common)
Concludes △ABD ≅ △ACD by AAS
Concludes AB = AC by CPCT

tasks.guidance: Accept other correct constructions, e.g. the perpendicular from A to BC (then AAS again). A proof that uses 'sides opposite equal angles are equal' is circular: it assumes the result.

tasks.prompt: In △PQR, S is the midpoint of QR and PS ⊥ QR. Prove that PQ = PR.

rubric.criterion: Chooses △PSQ and △PSR
QS = RS (S is the midpoint), ∠PSQ = ∠PSR = 90° (PS ⊥ QR), PS = PS (common)
Concludes △PSQ ≅ △PSR by SAS (the right angle is between the two sides)
Concludes PQ = PR by CPCT

tasks.guidance: Some learners will cite RHS; that needs the hypotenuses equal, which is what is being proved. SAS is the correct criterion here.

tasks.prompt: ABCD is a parallelogram whose diagonals AC and BD meet at O. Prove that O is the midpoint of both diagonals. You may use the fact that opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.

rubric.criterion: ∠OAB = ∠OCD and ∠OBA = ∠ODC, because they are alternate angles (AB ∥ DC)
AB = CD (opposite sides of a parallelogram)
Concludes △OAB ≅ △OCD by ASA (or AAS, using vertically opposite angles)
Concludes OA = OC and OB = OD by CPCT, so O bisects both diagonals

tasks.guidance: Check the vertex correspondence (A↔C, B↔D, O↔O). Vertically opposite angles at O may replace one pair of alternate angles.

tasks.prompt: In △ABC, AC² = AB² + BC². Prove that ∠B = 90°. (Hint: construct a right-angled triangle PQR with ∠Q = 90°, PQ = AB and QR = BC.)

rubric.criterion: Constructs △PQR with ∠Q = 90°, PQ = AB, QR = BC
Uses Pythagoras in △PQR: PR² = PQ² + QR² = AB² + BC² = AC², so PR = AC
Concludes △ABC ≅ △PQR by SSS
Concludes ∠B = ∠Q = 90° by CPCT

tasks.guidance: The key step is PR = AC (positive square roots of equal squares). Using the converse itself as a reason is circular.

tasks.prompt: Using only a ruler and compasses, construct an angle of 135° at a point O on a line. Explain why your angle is 135°. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Constructs the perpendicular to the line at O, making two right angles
Bisects one of the right angles (arc from O, equal arcs from the two cut points, join)
Identifies the 135° angle: between the bisector and the ray on the other side (90° + 45°, or 180° − 45°)
Explains why the bisector makes 45° (it halves 90°, by congruent triangles or equal distances)

tasks.guidance: Accept other correct routes, e.g. 120° + half of the 30° between 120° and 150°, if correctly justified. Check the learner names which angle is 135°. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Draw any triangle ABC whose angles are all less than 90°. Using a ruler and compasses, construct the circle that passes through A, B and C. Explain why it passes through all three corners. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Constructs the perpendicular bisector of one side, e.g. AB
Constructs the perpendicular bisector of a second side, e.g. BC, and marks the meeting point O
Draws the circle with centre O and radius OA
Explains: O is on the bisector of AB so OA = OB, and on the bisector of BC so OB = OC; so OA = OB = OC and the circle through A also passes through B and C

tasks.guidance: Two perpendicular bisectors are enough; the third may be drawn as a check. Credit 'equidistant from the endpoints' as the reason for each bisector. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct a triangle ABC with BC = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm and AB = 4 cm. Then construct a triangle similar to it whose sides are 2/3 of the corresponding sides of ABC, and explain why the new triangle is similar with scale factor 2/3. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Constructs △ABC by SSS
Draws a ray BX at an acute angle to BC (on the side away from A) and marks 3 equal steps B₁, B₂, B₃ with fixed compass opening
Joins B₃C and draws through B₂ a line parallel to B₃C, meeting BC at C′
Draws through C′ a line parallel to CA, meeting BA at A′
Explains: BC′/BC = BB₂/BB₃ = 2/3 (Basic Proportionality Theorem), and △A′BC′ ~ △ABC (AA, corresponding angles), so every side is 2/3

tasks.guidance: The parallels may be drawn by copying an angle with the compasses. The number of steps must be 3 (the larger of 2 and 3) and the join must be from B₃. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct any triangle PQR with QR = 5 cm. Then construct a triangle similar to PQR with scale factor 4/3 (each side 4/3 of the corresponding side of PQR). Explain why it has that scale factor. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws a ray QX at an acute angle to QR and marks 4 equal steps Q₁ … Q₄
Joins Q₃R (the 3rd mark, the denominator)
Through Q₄ draws a line parallel to Q₃R, meeting QR extended at R′
Through R′ draws a line parallel to RP, meeting QP extended at P′
Explains: QR′/QR = QQ₄/QQ₃ = 4/3, and △P′QR′ ~ △PQR (AA), so the scale factor is 4/3

tasks.guidance: The most common error is joining Q₄R and drawing the parallel through Q₃, which gives 3/4. QR and QP must be extended beyond R and P. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: To divide a segment AB in the ratio 2 : 3, Ravi draws a ray AX, marks 5 equal steps A₁ … A₅ on it, joins A₅B, and draws through A₂ a line parallel to A₅B, meeting AB at C. Explain why AC : CB = 2 : 3, and why the steps on AX must be equal.

rubric.criterion: States that A₂C ∥ A₅B in △AA₅B
Applies the Basic Proportionality Theorem: AC/CB = AA₂/A₂A₅
Uses equal steps: AA₂ = 2 steps and A₂A₅ = 3 steps, so AC : CB = 2 : 3
Explains that unequal steps would change the ratio AA₂ : A₂A₅, so the construction would fail

tasks.guidance: Accept a similar-triangles argument (△AA₂C ~ △AA₅B) in place of BPT.

tasks.prompt: Construct a trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC, AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm, ∠B = 60° and DC = 4 cm. Explain how you make DC parallel to AB. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws AB = 7 cm and makes ∠ABC = 60° with BC = 5 cm
Through C makes the line parallel to AB, e.g. by constructing ∠BCY = 120° on the same side as A
Marks CD = 4 cm along that line towards the side of A, and joins AD
Explains the parallel: the co-interior angles ∠B and ∠C add to 180° (or the corresponding/alternate angles are equal)

tasks.guidance: The point D must be marked in the direction of A. Any correct way of drawing the parallel through C is acceptable if it is explained. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct a quadrilateral ABCD with AB = 5.5 cm, BC = 4 cm, ∠A = 75°, ∠B = 100° and ∠C = 120° (a protractor may be used for the angles). Describe your steps, and say what ∠D will measure and why. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws AB = 5.5 cm and makes ∠A = 75° and ∠B = 100° on the same side
Marks BC = 4 cm on the arm from B
Makes ∠BCD = 120° at C; D is where this arm meets the arm from A
States ∠D = 360° − 75° − 100° − 120° = 65°, because the angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°

tasks.guidance: Check that the angle at C is measured inside the quadrilateral (from CB). The value of ∠D can be checked by measurement but must be justified by the angle sum. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Construct a rhombus whose diagonals are 8 cm and 6 cm. Explain why your construction gives a rhombus, and find the length of its side. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws one diagonal AC = 8 cm
Constructs the perpendicular bisector of AC and marks B and D on it, 3 cm on each side of the midpoint O
Explains: the diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so all four sides are equal (each point on the perpendicular bisector is equally far from A and C)
Finds the side by Pythagoras: √(4² + 3²) = 5 cm

tasks.guidance: Learners may use the property 'diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles' or the equal-distance property; both are full reasons. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Prove that √5 is irrational. Give the reason for each step.

rubric.criterion: Assumes √5 = a/b with a, b integers, b ≠ 0, with no common factor other than 1
Squares to get a² = 5b², so 5 divides a², and so 5 divides a (5 is prime)
Writes a = 5c, gets 25c² = 5b², so b² = 5c² and 5 divides b
States the contradiction (5 divides both a and b) and concludes √5 is irrational

tasks.guidance: The reason for '5 divides a² ⇒ 5 divides a' must refer to 5 being prime (or to prime factorisation). An argument by parity (even/odd) does not work for 5.

tasks.prompt: Given that √2 is irrational, prove that 1/√2 is irrational. Give the reason for each step.

rubric.criterion: Assumes 1/√2 = r, a rational number
Notes r ≠ 0 (since 1/√2 is not 0)
Rearranges to √2 = 1/r and explains that 1/r is rational (the reciprocal of a non-zero rational is rational)
States the contradiction with √2 being irrational, and concludes

tasks.guidance: An equivalent route: 1/√2 = √2/2; if it were rational r then √2 = 2r would be rational. Either needs the closure reason stated.

tasks.prompt: Describe how to draw the first three triangles of the square-root spiral, starting from a segment OA₁ of 1 unit, and explain why OA₂ = √2, OA₃ = √3 and OA₄ = √4 = 2. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws OA₁ = 1 unit, then A₁A₂ = 1 unit perpendicular to OA₁, and joins OA₂
At A₂ draws A₂A₃ = 1 unit perpendicular to OA₂ and joins OA₃; repeats at A₃ to get A₄
Uses Pythagoras each time: OA₂² = 1 + 1 = 2, OA₃² = 2 + 1 = 3, OA₄² = 3 + 1 = 4
States the general step: each new hypotenuse squared is one more than the last, so OAₙ = √n

tasks.guidance: Each unit segment must be perpendicular to the previous hypotenuse (not to OA₁). The perpendiculars may be constructed or drawn with a set square. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Describe how to construct a segment of length √3.5 using a ruler and compasses, by drawing AB = 3.5 units and BC = 1 unit on a straight line, a semicircle on AC, and a perpendicular at B. Explain why the perpendicular from B to the semicircle has length √3.5. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Draws AB = 3.5 and BC = 1 on one line, and finds the midpoint O of AC (by bisecting AC)
Draws the semicircle with centre O and radius OA = 2.25
Draws the perpendicular to AC at B, meeting the semicircle at D
Explains: OD = 2.25 (radius) and OB = 2.25 − 1 = 1.25, so BD² = OD² − OB² = 5.0625 − 1.5625 = 3.5

tasks.guidance: Accept the general argument: OD = (x + 1)/2, OB = (x − 1)/2, so BD² = x. The last step may be done with x = 3.5 or in general. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Locate √13 on the number line using a ruler and compasses, and explain why the point you mark is √13 from 0. Draw your construction with the straight edge and compass, and in the note list your steps in order. Your answer is marked on the steps you describe and on your reason why they work.

rubric.criterion: Chooses legs whose squares add to 13 (3 and 2): marks 3 on the number line and constructs a perpendicular of 2 units there
Joins 0 to the top of the perpendicular and uses Pythagoras: √(3² + 2²) = √13
Draws an arc centred at 0 through that point to meet the number line
Explains that the arc keeps the length: every point on it is √13 from 0

tasks.guidance: Any correct route is fine, e.g. legs √12 and 1 from an earlier construction. The arc must be centred at 0. Mark the drawing together with the steps in the note: a step counts when it is drawn or described and its arcs or lines are where they must be; a freehand drawing is judged on intent, not on precision.

tasks.prompt: Prove by mathematical induction that 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n² for every positive integer n.

rubric.criterion: Checks n = 1: 1 = 1²
Assumes P(k): 1 + 3 + … + (2k − 1) = k²
Adds the next term 2k + 1 and shows k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)², using the hypothesis
Concludes by the principle of mathematical induction

tasks.guidance: The (k + 1)-th odd number is 2(k + 1) − 1 = 2k + 1; check the learner adds this term and not 2k − 1 again.

tasks.prompt: Prove by mathematical induction that 2ⁿ > n for every positive integer n.

rubric.criterion: Checks n = 1: 2 > 1
Assumes 2ᵏ > k for some positive integer k
Shows 2ᵏ⁺¹ = 2 · 2ᵏ > 2k ≥ k + 1 (since k ≥ 1), so 2ᵏ⁺¹ > k + 1
Concludes by induction

tasks.guidance: The step needs the reason 2k ≥ k + 1 because k ≥ 1; without it the chain of inequalities is incomplete.

tasks.prompt: A pile has 17 counters. Two players take turns to take 1, 2, 3 or 4 counters. Whoever takes the last counter wins. Would you rather go first or second? Explain a strategy that always wins, whatever the other player does.

rubric.criterion: Finds the safe numbers to leave: multiples of 5 (15, 10, 5, 0)
Chooses to go first and take 2, leaving 15
Explains answering every move: if the other player takes t, you take 5 − t, so each round removes 5
Explains why this always works: you always leave a multiple of 5, so you take the last counter

tasks.guidance: A learner who finds the 'make each round 5' rule but takes the wrong first move gets the strategy marks; feedback should show 17 = 3 × 5 + 2.

tasks.prompt: There are 14 matches. Two players take turns to take 1, 2 or 3 matches. This time, whoever takes the LAST match LOSES. Would you go first or second? Explain a strategy that always wins.

rubric.criterion: Sees that you want to leave the other player 1 match, so the safe numbers to leave are 1, 5, 9, 13
Chooses to go first and take 1, leaving 13
Explains answering each move t with 4 − t, so each round removes 4
Explains that the other player is finally left with 1 match and must take it

tasks.guidance: This changes the target from 0 to 1; reward learners who adapt the 'leave a multiple of 4' idea to 'leave one more than a multiple of 4'.

tasks.prompt: A running total starts at 0. Two players take turns to add 1, 2, 3 or 4 to it. Whoever makes the total exactly 25 wins. Would you rather go first or second? Explain a strategy that always wins.

rubric.criterion: Finds the safe totals: 25, 20, 15, 10, 5 (multiples of 5)
Sees that the first player cannot reach 5 in one go (the most they can add is 4), so chooses to go second
Explains answering every addition t with 5 − t, so the total after each of your turns is a multiple of 5
Explains why this reaches 25 on your turn whatever the other player does

tasks.guidance: The twist is that going second wins here. Credit any clear explanation, in words, a table, or a worked game with the general rule stated.

tasks.prompt: A school newsletter shows a bar graph titled 'Our results are soaring!'. The bars show pass percentages: 2023: 91%, 2024: 93%, 2025: 95%. The vertical axis starts at 90%, so the 2025 bar looks five times as tall as the 2023 bar. There are no axis labels. Explain at least two ways the graph could mislead a reader, and describe how you would redraw it.

rubric.criterion: Explains that starting the axis at 90% makes the bars' heights out of proportion (2023 bar 1 unit, 2025 bar 5 units, though 95 is not 5 times 91)
Points out a second problem: no axis labels, or a title that overstates the change
Describes a fair redesign: axis from 0 (or a clearly marked break), labelled axes with units, a neutral title
States what the data really shows: a small, steady rise of 2 percentage points a year

tasks.guidance: Accept other valid criticisms. A redesign that keeps the axis break is fine if the break is clearly marked and the learner says why.

tasks.prompt: For each data set, name a suitable display and give one reason: (a) how the 36 students in a class travel to school (walk, cycle, bus, car); (b) the temperature in your town at noon each day for two weeks; (c) the number of books read by boys and by girls in each of Classes 6, 7 and 8.

rubric.criterion: (a) Pie chart or bar graph, with a reason (parts of one whole / comparing categories)
(b) Line graph, because it shows change over time
(c) Double bar graph, because it compares two groups across the same categories
Reasons are about the kind of data and the question, not just 'it looks nice'

tasks.guidance: Accept a bar graph for (a) and (b) if well justified (e.g. bars for daily values). A pie chart for (b) or (c) is not suitable: the values are not parts of one whole.

tasks.prompt: A family recorded the water they used in one week: drinking and cooking 70 L, bathing 280 L, washing clothes 210 L, cleaning 140 L. Describe in words a clear display of this data that you would make: the kind of display, the title, what goes on each axis or in each sector, the scale or the angles, and any key. Explain your choices.

rubric.criterion: Chooses a suitable display (bar graph or pie chart) and says why
Gives a clear title and labels (axes with units, or labelled sectors)
Gives a correct scale (e.g. 1 cm = 50 L) or correct angles (total 700 L: 36°, 144°, 108°, 72°)
Mentions a fair choice such as an axis from 0 or equal bar widths

tasks.guidance: There is no drawing tool, so mark the description. For a pie chart the angles are 70/700 × 360 = 36°, 144°, 108°, 72°.

tasks.prompt: An advert shows a 3-D pie chart titled 'What people choose'. The sectors are labelled Brand A 50%, Brand B 35% and Others 25%. The Brand A slice is pulled out and drawn in front, and there is no information about who was asked or how many. Explain what is wrong or unclear with this display and how it should be improved.

rubric.criterion: Notices the percentages add to 110%, which is impossible for parts of one whole
Explains that the 3-D, pulled-out slice makes Brand A look bigger than its share
Points out that the sample (who and how many were asked) is missing, so the claim cannot be judged
Suggests improvements: a flat chart or bar graph with correct percentages, a source and sample size, a clear title

tasks.guidance: Any three well-explained problems with sensible improvements deserve full marks.

tasks.prompt: These questions are not statistical: (a) How tall am I? (b) What time does our school start? (c) How many pages does my maths book have? Rewrite each one as a statistical question, and explain what makes your new questions statistical.

rubric.criterion: Rewrites (a) as a question about many people, e.g. 'How tall are the students in Class 7?'
Rewrites (b) and (c) as questions whose answers come from data that varies (e.g. 'What time do students in our class wake up?', 'How many pages do the books in our class library have?')
Explains that a statistical question is answered by collecting data that varies, not by one fixed fact

tasks.guidance: Any sensible rewrites are fine as long as the answer needs data with variability.

tasks.prompt: You want to find out: 'How much time do students in our school spend on screens on a school day?' Plan the investigation: who you will ask and how many, exactly what you will ask or measure, how you will record and display the data, and one thing that could make your conclusion unreliable.

rubric.criterion: Chooses a sensible sample (e.g. students from every class, not only friends) and a number
States exactly what is measured, with units (e.g. minutes yesterday, a school day)
Describes how the data will be recorded and displayed (tally/frequency table, bar graph of grouped times)
Names a real limitation (self-reported estimates, a small or unrepresentative sample, an unusual day)

tasks.guidance: Reward precise questions ('How many minutes did you spend on a phone, TV or computer yesterday after school?') over vague ones ('Do you use screens a lot?').

tasks.prompt: Minutes spent reading on one day by 10 students in each class: Class 7A: 20, 25, 30, 30, 35, 40, 40, 45, 50, 65. Class 7B: 10, 15, 20, 30, 30, 35, 35, 40, 60, 75. Which class read more that day? Support your answer with at least two measures (such as mean, median or range), and give one reason to be careful with your conclusion.

rubric.criterion: Finds the means correctly: 7A 38 minutes, 7B 35 minutes
Finds the medians (7A 37.5, 7B 32.5) or the ranges (7A 45, 7B 65) correctly
Concludes that 7A read a little more on average that day, and that 7B's times were more spread out
Gives a sensible caution: only one day, only 10 students, small differences, or self-reported times

tasks.guidance: A conclusion that only says '7A' without evidence earns at most one mark. Accept 'about the same' if it is argued from the small difference and the spread.

tasks.prompt: A tea shop puts up a sign: 'Most people in our town prefer our tea!' They asked 12 customers inside the shop, and 9 said they preferred its tea. Is the claim supported by this data? Explain, and say what data would be needed to test the claim properly.

rubric.criterion: Explains that the people asked were already the shop's customers, so they are not representative of the town
Explains that 12 people is too few to speak for a whole town
States what the data does support (9 of the 12 customers asked preferred the tea)
Describes better data: a larger random sample of people across the town, asked a fair question

tasks.guidance: Look for the idea that a conclusion can only be as wide as the group the data came from.

tasks.prompt: Anu and Ravi measure the same mat with their own hand spans. Before measuring, Anu guessed 5 spans. Then Anu counted 6 spans and Ravi counted 8 spans. (1) Was Anu's guess close? How do you know? (2) Why did Anu and Ravi get different numbers for the same mat? (3) What could they both use so that they get the same number?

rubric.criterion: Compares the guess with the count: says the guess was close (only 1 span less, or 'a little short')
Explains that their hand spans are different sizes (Ravi's span is smaller, so he needs more of them)
Suggests one thing that is the same for both, e.g. a ruler, a metre scale or tape in centimetres, or the same pencil or string

tasks.guidance: A complete answer has all three parts. Accept informal words: 'Ravi has small hands', 'her hands are bigger'. For (3) any shared unit earns the point (one person's span used by both, the same stick, a ruler); the idea is that the unit must not change. A child who says only 'use a ruler' with no reason still earns the point for (3). Do not take a point off for spelling or for an answer an adult wrote down from the child's words.

tasks.prompt: Choose something long at home or at school: a table, a bed, a door or a mat. (1) First guess how many of your hand spans long it is, and write your guess. (2) Then measure it with your hand spans (or say how you would measure it). (3) Write the number you got. Was your guess too big, too small or close? By how much?

rubric.criterion: Names the object and writes a guess as a number of spans (or another informal unit) before the measurement
Gives a measured number of spans, or describes measuring sensibly (start at one end, put spans end to end with no gaps, count them)
Compares the guess with the measurement correctly: too big, too small or close, with the difference if asked

tasks.guidance: The marker cannot see the object, so mark the reasoning, not the real length. The comparison must agree with the child's own two numbers (guess 6, measured 9: 'too small by 3'). An older child (Grade 4) may use a ruler and centimetres; that is fine. A child who only writes one number earns at most one point. Informal words like 'nearly right' are acceptable for 'close'.

tasks.prompt: Kavin guessed that his water bottle would fill 5 glasses. When he poured it out, it filled only 3 glasses. Now he has a jug that looks about twice as big as his bottle. (1) Was his first guess too big or too small? (2) How many glasses should he guess for the jug, and why? (3) How can he check his new guess?

rubric.criterion: Says the first guess (5) was too big, because only 3 glasses were filled
Gives a sensible guess for the jug that uses what he learned (about 6 glasses, because the jug is about twice the bottle, which held 3)
Describes checking by pouring the jug into glasses of the same size and counting them

tasks.guidance: For (2) accept 5, 6 or 7 glasses if the child links it to the bottle holding 3 ('double of 3'). A guess with no reason, or one still based on 5, does not earn the point. For (3) the child should say the glasses are the same size or 'the same glass'; pouring and counting is the key idea. Informal language is fine.

tasks.prompt: Make your own repeating pattern! Use at least two different shapes, such as circles, squares and triangles. Draw it in a row so that it repeats at least 3 times. In the note, tell which part repeats.

rubric.criterion: The drawing shows a pattern in which the same group of shapes repeats at least 3 times without a mistake
The pattern uses at least two different shapes (or two sizes or turns of a shape)
The note names or describes the part that repeats (e.g. 'circle, square, square, then again')

tasks.guidance: Any repeating pattern counts, e.g. circle-triangle-circle-triangle, or big-small-small. Rough hand-drawn shapes are fine as long as the shapes can be told apart. If the pattern breaks once (a shape missing), do not give the 'repeat' point. A young child may say 'it goes round, square, round, square' in the note: that names the repeating part. A pattern that grows (more shapes each time) is not a repeating pattern.

tasks.prompt: Meena is drawing a rangoli border. She draws arrows in a row: the 1st arrow points up, the 2nd points right, the 3rd points down, the 4th points left, the 5th points up again. Draw the first 5 arrows and then the next 4 arrows. In the note, say how each arrow changes from the one before, and which way the 12th arrow points.

rubric.criterion: Draws the 5 arrows as described and continues with 4 correct arrows (right, down, left, up)
Describes the change: each arrow turns a quarter turn (a right angle) clockwise, or 'it turns like a clock hand', or names the repeating group of 4 arrows
Says the 12th arrow points left, with any sensible reason (every 4th arrow points left; 4, 8, 12)

tasks.guidance: Arrows 6 to 9 are right, down, left, up. The 12th arrow points left (arrows 4, 8 and 12 all point left). Accept 'turns to the right each time', 'goes round' or 'up, right, down, left again' for the rule. A child who draws more arrows to find the 12th has used a good method; give the point if the answer is left.

tasks.prompt: Kavin tidied his toy box. He found these toys, one at a time: ball, car, block, ball, block, block, car, ball, block. Draw one small picture or one mark for each toy. Put the balls in one row, the cars in another row and the blocks in another row. In the note, write which toy he has the most of.

rubric.criterion: Makes a separate row (or group) for each kind of toy: balls, cars and blocks
Has the right number of pictures or marks in each row: 3 balls, 2 cars, 4 blocks
Says blocks are the most

tasks.guidance: Pictures can be very simple (circles for balls, squares for blocks) or plain strokes. The rows should be labelled in some way: a little picture at the start, a letter, or the note. Lining the marks up so the rows are easy to compare is good practice but not required. If one count is off by one, withhold only the 'count' point.

tasks.prompt: Fatima asked her friends, 'Which fruit do you like best?' The answers were: mango, banana, mango, guava, mango, banana, mango. Draw a table with one row for each fruit. Next to each fruit, put a mark for every friend who chose it, and then write the number. In the note, say how many more friends chose mango than banana.

rubric.criterion: Draws a table with a row (or column) for each fruit named once: mango, banana, guava
Records the right marks or numbers: mango 4, banana 2, guava 1
Says 2 more friends chose mango than banana

tasks.guidance: The table can be drawn with straight lines on the squared sheet, or simply be three neat rows with labels. Accept tally marks, dots, little pictures or numerals. A child who only lists the fruits without counts earns the 'table' point only. For the comparison, accept '2 more' or 'mango 4, banana 2, so 2'.

tasks.prompt: Class 4 children were asked, 'How do you come to school?' Here are their 20 answers: bus, walk, walk, cycle, bus, auto, walk, bus, bus, walk, cycle, walk, bus, auto, walk, bus, cycle, walk, bus, walk. Make a frequency table with three columns: way of coming, tally marks, and number of children. In the note, say which way is the most common and how you checked that you counted all 20.

rubric.criterion: Draws a table with the three columns and one row for each way (bus, walk, cycle, auto)
Uses tally marks grouped in fives (four strokes crossed by a fifth)
Gives the right numbers: bus 7, walk 8, cycle 3, auto 2
Names walking as the most common and checks the total: 7 + 8 + 3 + 2 = 20 (or another sensible check)

tasks.guidance: Correct counts: bus 7, walk 8, cycle 3, auto 2 (total 20). Tallies drawn as |||| with a crossing stroke for 5 earn the tally point; plain strokes without grouping do not. The check point needs both the most common way and a check (adding the totals, or ticking off each answer). If one count is wrong but the child's total check reveals it, still withhold the 'numbers' point.

tasks.prompt: (1) Ravi puts a dice on paper and draws around its bottom. Then he does the same with a round tin can standing up. Draw the two shapes he gets. (2) Now join points with straight lines to make a triangle and a rectangle that is not a square. In the note, write the name of each shape you drew.

rubric.criterion: Draws a square for the bottom of the dice and names it a square
Draws a circle for the bottom of the tin can and names it a circle
Draws a closed triangle with three straight sides
Draws a closed rectangle with two long and two short sides (not a square), with square corners

tasks.guidance: Shapes drawn by hand need not be perfect; a square that is a little uneven is fine if the child names it a square. Using the straight edge on the squared sheet, joining grid corners, is the expected way for part (2). A 'rectangle' with all four sides equal is a square and does not earn the rectangle point. A young child may say 'round' for circle and 'box shape' for square; accept these.

tasks.prompt: Sort these into flat shapes and solid shapes: a ball, a triangle drawn on the blackboard, a brick, a ladoo, a square drawn in chalk on the floor, a tin can. Then explain in your own words how a flat shape is different from a solid shape.

rubric.criterion: Puts the triangle on the board and the chalk square in the flat group
Puts the ball, brick, ladoo and tin can in the solid group
Explains the difference, e.g. a solid can be picked up or held and has thickness (takes up space); a flat shape lies on a surface and has only length and width

tasks.guidance: Accept informal explanations: 'you can hold a solid but not a drawing', 'solid things are fat', 'flat shapes are only on paper'. Naming solids (sphere, cuboid, cylinder) is a bonus, not required. If one object is in the wrong group, withhold the point for that group only.

tasks.prompt: Draw three straight lines: one standing straight up and down, one lying flat from side to side, and one slanting. Then use only straight lines to draw a picture, such as a house, a kite or a boat. In the note, tell which lines in your picture are up-and-down, side-to-side or slanting.

rubric.criterion: Draws one vertical, one horizontal and one slanting straight line
Draws a picture made only of straight lines
The note correctly points out at least one line of each direction in the picture (e.g. the walls are up and down, the roof is slanting)

tasks.guidance: Lines drawn with the straight edge are expected. Accept the child's own words: 'standing line', 'sleeping line', 'leaning line', 'slope'. A line that is only a little tilted from vertical can still count as up-and-down if the child clearly meant it. The picture does not have to be neat.

tasks.prompt: The picture shows how many fruits Anu sold at her stall this morning. (1) Which fruit did she sell the most of? (2) Which the fewest? (3) Tomorrow Anu can bring more of only one fruit. Which should she bring, and why?

rubric.criterion: Says mangoes sold the most
Says apples sold the fewest
Chooses a fruit and gives a reason that uses the data (e.g. mangoes, because most people bought them and she may run out)

tasks.guidance: Counts in the picture: mango 7, banana 5, guava 3, apple 2. For (3), mango with the reason 'most people want them' is the expected answer, but accept another fruit if the reason is sensible and uses the data (e.g. 'guava, because she sold all she had'). A choice with no reason does not earn the point.

tasks.prompt: The table shows how many library books Class 5 read each day. Draw a pictograph of it, using one picture of a book for 10 books. Write the key, and label each day. In the note, explain how you showed the days that are not a whole number of tens.

rubric.criterion: Writes a key: one book picture = 10 books
Draws the right number of whole book pictures: Monday 3, Tuesday 1, Wednesday 1, Thursday 2
Shows 15 and 25 with a half picture (Tuesday 1½, Thursday 2½) and explains it stands for 5 books
Labels every row (or column) with its day

tasks.guidance: Correct rows: Monday 30 = 3 books, Tuesday 15 = 1½, Wednesday 10 = 1, Thursday 25 = 2½. A half can be drawn as a book cut in half or clearly marked as half. The key must be written; a pictograph without a key loses only the key point. A child who uses a different key (e.g. one picture = 5 books) with correct counts should get every point except 'half'.

tasks.prompt: Ravi wants to tile a floor using copies of one tile that is NOT a square. Choose a tile shape (for example a triangle, an L-shape or a long rectangle). Cover a part of the sheet that is at least 4 squares by 4 squares with your tile, with no gaps and no tiles on top of each other. In the note, describe the part that repeats and whether you slid, flipped or turned the tile to make it fit.

rubric.criterion: The tiles cover a region of at least 4 by 4 squares
There are no gaps and no overlaps between the tiles
Every tile is the same shape and size, and the shape is not a square
The note describes the repeating unit and says how the tile was moved (slid, flipped or turned)

tasks.guidance: Easy correct answers: rectangles 1 by 2 laid like bricks; right triangles made by cutting each square along a diagonal; L-shapes of 3 squares fitted in pairs. The edges of the region may be ragged if the child explains that the tiles would be cut at the wall. Accept 'moved it along', 'turned it round', 'upside down' as informal names for slide, turn and flip.

tasks.prompt: Fatima wants to tile her floor with tiles that are all the same regular shape. She can buy equilateral triangles, squares, regular pentagons or regular hexagons. Which of these can cover the floor with no gaps and no overlaps? Explain using the angles that meet at one corner point.

rubric.criterion: Names the triangle, square and hexagon as shapes that tile
Says the regular pentagon does not tile
Explains the pentagon fails because its angle (108°) does not fit exactly into 360° (3 make 324°, leaving a gap; 4 make 432°, an overlap)

tasks.guidance: The key idea is that the angles meeting at a point must add to exactly 360°. Interior angles: triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°. A child who draws pentagons and shows a gap, without angles, may get the 'pentagon' point but not 'reason'. Accept 'a full turn' for 360°.

tasks.prompt: Draw three angles by joining points with straight lines: a right angle, an acute angle and an obtuse angle. In the note, write which is which and explain how you can tell an acute angle and an obtuse angle apart from a right angle.

rubric.criterion: Draws a right angle (square corner) correctly
Draws an acute angle (smaller than a right angle) and labels it acute
Draws an obtuse angle (bigger than a right angle but less than a straight line) and labels it obtuse
Explains comparing each angle with a right angle, e.g. using the corner of a page or a square on the grid

tasks.guidance: Using the grid lines makes the right angle easy; diagonals make 45° or 135° angles. An 'obtuse' angle that is a straight line does not count. Accept 'narrow/sharp' for acute and 'wide/open' for obtuse when it is clear they are compared with a square corner.

tasks.prompt: (1) Meena says, 'A square is not a rectangle.' Ravi says, 'A square is a special rectangle.' Who is right? Explain using sides and corners. (2) Can a triangle have two right angles? Explain. (3) Kavin makes a triangle and a square from straws joined at the corners. When he pushes a corner, which one changes shape and which one stays the same?

rubric.criterion: Says Ravi is right because a square has four right-angle corners and opposite sides equal, like every rectangle (its sides are all equal as well)
Says a triangle can have at most one right angle, with a reason (e.g. two right angles would make two sides go straight up and never meet, or the three angles would be too big)
Says the straw square can be pushed out of shape (into a slanting shape) but the triangle stays the same

tasks.guidance: For (1) the explanation must mention the corners (all right angles); 'because it has four sides' alone is not enough. For (2) a drawing described in words is fine: 'the two sides would be parallel'. Grade 4 children will not know the angle sum; any sensible reason earns the point. For (3) 'the square goes flat/squashes' is fine.

tasks.prompt: Ravi builds with 4 cube blocks. He puts 3 blocks in a row on the floor, and the 4th block on top of the block at the left end. Draw what you see from the front, and what you see from the top. In the note, label which drawing is which.

rubric.criterion: Front view: three squares in a row with one square on top of the left square
Top view: three squares in a row (the top block hides the one under it)
The two views are labelled correctly

tasks.guidance: Front view looks like an L turned over: 3 squares across with 1 square above the left one. The top view is just 3 squares in a row. A common mistake is to draw 4 squares in the top view; explain kindly that the top block covers the one underneath. Small differences in square size are fine. A child who draws a 3D picture instead of a flat view does not earn that view's point.

tasks.prompt: The picture is a map of Kavin's village seen from the top. The lines are roads, and the top of the map is north. Write directions for Kavin to walk from Home to School along the roads. Say which way he starts, where he turns left or right, and the places he passes.

rubric.criterion: Gives a correct starting direction along a road from Home (east towards the Temple, or north towards the Park)
Gives a correct turn at a corner (e.g. at the end of the road turn left, to the north), with left or right correct for the way he is walking
Names at least one place he passes on the way that is really on that route (Temple, Market, Well or Park)
The route reaches the School

tasks.guidance: Two shortest routes: east past the Temple to the corner, turn left (north), past the Market to the School; or north to the Park, turn right (east) along the top road to the School. A route along the middle road past the Well is also acceptable. Accept north, south, east, west or left and right; check left/right from the walker's point of view. Using the grid numbers ('go to 6') instead of directions earns the start point only if the way is clear.

tasks.prompt: Draw a plan of your classroom or of one room at home, as if you were looking down from the ceiling. Show the door, a window and at least three things in the room (such as a table, a bed or a cupboard) in the right places. In the note, name each thing and write how to walk from the door to one of them.

rubric.criterion: The drawing is a top view: things are drawn as flat outlines (rectangles for tables, beds), not side pictures
Shows the door, a window and at least three named things
Things are placed sensibly (e.g. door and window on the walls, furniture inside the room)
The note gives a route from the door with direction words such as straight, left, right, next to, past

tasks.guidance: The marker cannot check the real room, so look for a plan that makes sense. Labels may be in the note (e.g. '1 = bed, 2 = table'). Small side pictures of a chair are acceptable if the rest is a top view; a whole picture drawn from the front does not earn the 'top' point. The route must match the drawing.

tasks.prompt: On a 1 to 100 number grid (rows of ten: 1–10, 11–20, and so on), Fatima colours 4, 13, 22, 31. (1) What is the rule? (2) Which three numbers will she colour next? (3) Her coloured squares make a slanting line on the grid. Explain why.

rubric.criterion: States the rule: add 9 each time
Gives the next three numbers: 40, 49, 58
Explains the slant: adding 9 is like going down one row (add 10) and back one place (take away 1)

tasks.guidance: Accept 'it goes up by 9' or 'the tens go up 1 and the ones go down 1' for the rule (that also explains the pattern). For (3) the child must link the move on the grid to adding 10 and taking 1 (down one, left one). A child who only says 'because it goes like that' does not earn the 'why' point.

tasks.prompt: Here is a pattern of squares. Step 1 is 1 square. Step 2 is an L shape of 3 squares: one square with one more on top and one more on the right. Step 3 is a bigger L of 5 squares. Draw steps 1, 2 and 3, then draw steps 4 and 5. In the note, write the rule in words and say how many squares step 10 will have.

rubric.criterion: Draws steps 4 and 5 correctly as L shapes of 7 and 9 squares, each arm one square longer
Writes the rule in words: each step adds 2 squares, one on each arm (or 'the arms get one longer')
Says step 10 has 19 squares, with a reason (counting on by 2, or 10 + 9)

tasks.guidance: Squares: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, ... step n has 2n − 1 squares, so step 10 has 19. Accept 'add 2 each time' or 'it goes up in odd numbers' for the rule. A child who continues drawing up to step 10 and counts is using a good method. If steps 4 and 5 have the right counts but are not L shapes, give the 'draw' point only if they still grow the same way.

tasks.prompt: Draw three squares of the same size, each 4 squares long and 4 squares wide. Divide each one into quarters (4 equal parts), using a different way for each square. In the note, explain how you know the parts in each square are equal.

rubric.criterion: Draws three same-size squares, each split into 4 parts
In every square, the 4 parts are equal (same number of small squares, or the same shape)
The three ways are different (e.g. four strips, four small squares, four triangles from the diagonals)
Explains equality, e.g. by counting 4 small squares in each part, or by saying the parts match if one is moved onto another

tasks.guidance: Common correct ways: 4 columns of 1 × 4; 4 small 2 × 2 squares; both diagonals (4 triangles); 4 L-shapes of 4 squares. Parts may be different shapes inside one square as long as each has 4 small squares, if the child explains that. A split into 4 unequal parts does not earn the 'equal' point.

tasks.prompt: Ravi cuts a small roti into two equal halves. Anu cuts a big roti into two equal halves. Ravi says, 'My half is the same as Anu's half, because both are halves.' Is Ravi right? Explain why or why not.

rubric.criterion: Says Ravi is not right: Anu's half is bigger
Explains that the size of a half depends on the size of the whole: half of a big roti is more than half of a small roti

tasks.guidance: The key idea: halves can only be compared when they come from the same whole (or wholes of the same size). Accept 'her roti was bigger, so her piece is bigger'. A child who says 'both are half, so the same' has the common misconception; give no points. A child may add 'they are the same part of their own roti': that is a good extra, not required.

tasks.prompt: The side of one small square on the sheet is 1 unit. Draw two different shapes along the grid lines that each have a perimeter (the length all the way round the edge) of 12 units. In the note, show how you counted the perimeter of each. Then answer: Meena wants to sew lace around the edge of a tablecloth. Does she need to know its perimeter or its area? Why?

rubric.criterion: The first shape has a perimeter of exactly 12 units
A second, different shape also has a perimeter of exactly 12 units
The note shows the counting (e.g. 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 12, or counting unit edges)
Says perimeter, because the lace goes around the edge, not over the whole cloth

tasks.guidance: Shapes with perimeter 12: 3 × 3 square, 2 × 4 and 1 × 5 rectangles, and many L-shapes (e.g. an L inside a 3 × 3 box). A 4 × 2 rectangle turned is the same shape as 2 × 4. Children often count squares inside (area) instead of edges: check the counting. Accept 'the outside' or 'the boundary' for the reason.

tasks.prompt: Kavin says, 'When I add two odd numbers, the answer is always odd.' Try at least three examples. Is Kavin right? Explain why, for example by thinking of the numbers as dots put in pairs.

rubric.criterion: Gives at least three correct examples of adding two odd numbers (e.g. 3 + 5 = 8, 7 + 9 = 16, 1 + 1 = 2)
Says Kavin is wrong: odd + odd is always even
Explains with pairs: each odd number has one left over, and the two left-over ones make a new pair, so nothing is left over

tasks.guidance: The examples must be correct sums of two odd numbers. For 'why', accept a description of dots or counters in pairs, or 'the two extra ones join up'. 'Because the examples are even' is not an explanation of why it is ALWAYS even; it earns the verdict point only.

tasks.prompt: Anu and Ravi play a game. They start at 0 and take turns. On each turn a player adds 1 or 2 to the total and says the new total. Whoever says 10 wins. Anu goes first. How can Anu make sure she always wins? Explain your plan.

rubric.criterion: Finds the safe totals for Anu: 1, 4, 7 and 10
Says Anu should start by saying 1
Explains the reply: whatever Ravi adds, Anu adds the other number so the two moves make 3 (Ravi 1, Anu 2; Ravi 2, Anu 1)
Explains why it works: from 7, Ravi can only reach 8 or 9, and then Anu can reach 10 (working backwards from 10 in jumps of 3)

tasks.guidance: Full answer: say 1, then always make the total 4, 7, then 10 by adding so that each round makes 3. Accept a worked example game plus 'always make it add up to 3 with Ravi'. A child who only says 'go first' or 'add 2 every time' has not found the strategy.

tasks.prompt: The picture shows half of a temple design. The straight line going up from 4 is the fold line. Copy the half and the fold line onto the squared sheet, then draw the other half so that the whole design is symmetrical about the fold line. In the note, say how you made sure the two halves match.

rubric.criterion: Copies the given half and the fold line correctly
Draws the other half as a mirror image: each corner is the same number of squares from the fold line, on the other side
Explains the method, e.g. counting squares across from the fold line for each corner

tasks.guidance: The completed design has corners (in figure units) at (6, 1), (6, 4), (7, 4) and back to the top at (4, 7). On the sketch pad the scale can differ: check that each corner on the new half is as far from the fold line as its partner. A common mistake is to copy the half shifted instead of flipped (the slanting roof then leans the wrong way). Accept 'I counted the boxes' as the method.

tasks.prompt: Draw the letters A, H and N, and a square, using straight lines. On each one, draw every line of symmetry you can find. Some may have more than one, some may have none. In the note, write how many lines of symmetry each one has and how you checked.

rubric.criterion: Draws one vertical line of symmetry on A
Draws two lines of symmetry on H (up-down and across)
Says N has no line of symmetry
Draws all four lines of symmetry on the square (two through the middles of opposite sides, two along the diagonals)
Explains a check, e.g. imagining folding along the line and the halves matching, or using a mirror

tasks.guidance: A has 1, H has 2, N has 0 (it has turning symmetry, which is not a line of symmetry), the square has 4. The commonest mistake is to miss the diagonals of the square, or to give N a slanting line. Lines drawn a little off-centre are fine if the intention is clear. Folding in the imagination is a fine check.

tasks.prompt: Kavin counted the birds he saw in his garden one morning (see the table). Draw a bar graph of his counts. Give it a title, name each bar, and number the side so the height of each bar can be read. In the note, say which bird he saw most often and how many more crows than parrots he saw.

rubric.criterion: Draws four bars with the right heights: crow 6, sparrow 4, parrot 2, myna 5
Names each bar and numbers the side (the scale starts at 0 and goes up evenly)
Gives the graph a title
Says crows were seen most, and 4 more crows than parrots

tasks.guidance: One square for one bird is the easiest scale. Bars should have equal width and start from the same base line; gaps between bars are usual. Bars drawn as columns of tally marks do not count as a bar graph. Labels may be first letters or written in the note if they clearly match the bars.

tasks.prompt: The table shows the tickets sold at a school fair. Draw a bar graph using a scale of one square for 5 tickets. Write the scale on your graph. In the note: (1) find the total number of tickets sold, (2) how many more were sold on the best day than on the worst day, and (3) say how many you think will be sold on Friday, and why.

rubric.criterion: Uses and writes the scale 1 square = 5 tickets, with the side numbered 0, 5, 10, ...
Draws bars of the right heights: Monday 4 squares, Tuesday 7, Wednesday 10, Thursday 5
Total is 130 tickets
Difference is 30 (Wednesday 50 − Monday 20)
Gives a prediction with a reason taken from the graph (e.g. about 30, between the usual days; or more, because Friday is the last day)

tasks.guidance: Values: 20, 35, 50, 25; total 130; most − least = 50 − 20 = 30. Tuesday's bar is 7 squares (35 ÷ 5). Any sensible prediction with a reason from the data earns the last point; there is no single right answer. A graph with one square for 1 ticket will not fit the sheet; if the child used a different but clearly stated scale and correct heights, give the 'bars' point and not the 'scale' point.

tasks.prompt: Meena guesses that her pencil is 12 cm long. To check, she puts one end of the pencil at the 1 cm mark of her ruler (not at 0). The other end is at the 16 cm mark. (1) Is the pencil 16 cm long? Explain. (2) How long is it really, in centimetres and in millimetres? (3) Was her guess too long or too short, and by how much?

rubric.criterion: Explains that 16 is not the length because she started at 1, not 0
Gives the real length: 15 cm, which is 150 mm
Says the guess was too short by 3 cm

tasks.guidance: Length = 16 − 1 = 15 cm = 150 mm. Accept 'count the centimetres between the two ends' as the explanation. If the child gets 15 cm but not 150 mm, still give the 'length' point at Grade 4 but note it in feedback. The guess comparison should follow the child's own length (e.g. if they said 16, then 'too short by 4' is consistent but the 'start' and 'length' points are lost).

tasks.prompt: Make up your own story problem about shopping at a market with ₹100. It must need two steps to solve (for example, first add the prices, then find the change). Write the problem, then solve it, showing each step and the answer.

rubric.criterion: Writes a clear story problem about money that needs two different steps
Shows both steps separately with the right operations
Gets the right answer to their own problem and says what it means (e.g. 'Ravi gets ₹28 back')

tasks.guidance: Example: 'Anu buys mangoes for ₹45 and bananas for ₹27 with a ₹100 note. How much change?' 45 + 27 = 72, then 100 − 72 = 28. A one-step problem earns at most the 'answer' point. Amounts that cost more than ₹100 should be noticed in feedback but are fine if the child handles them sensibly.

tasks.prompt: Anu and Ravi both find 25 × 12. Anu does 25 × 10 and 25 × 2, then adds. Ravi does 25 × 4, then multiplies that answer by 3. (1) Work out each person's way, step by step. (2) Do they get the same answer? (3) Which way do you think is quicker, and why?

rubric.criterion: Works Anu's way: 250 + 50 = 300
Works Ravi's way: 100 × 3 = 300
Picks a way and gives a reason (e.g. Ravi's is quicker because 25 × 4 = 100 is easy and multiplying 100 by 3 is easy)

tasks.guidance: Both give 300. For (3) either choice is acceptable with a sensible reason: Anu's 'because ×10 is easy' is as valid as Ravi's 'because it makes 100'. The point is for comparing the ways, not for a particular choice.

tasks.prompt: In Class 4, half of the children like cricket best, one quarter like kabaddi best and one quarter like kho-kho best. Use the compass to draw a circle, then divide it to make a pie chart of this. In the note, say which part is which. Then answer: if there are 40 children, how many like kabaddi best?

rubric.criterion: Draws a circle with a centre and divides it with straight lines from the centre
Shows one half and two quarters (a diameter, and a radius at a right angle to it in one half)
The note matches each part to the right game (half for cricket, quarters for kabaddi and kho-kho)
Says 10 children like kabaddi

tasks.guidance: A good drawing: one diameter splits the circle in half (cricket); a radius at right angles splits the other half into two quarters. Parts that are roughly but not exactly equal are fine for a hand drawing. Quarter of 40 is 10. A child who splits the circle into three equal parts has missed the idea of half and quarter; withhold 'parts'.

tasks.prompt: Make your own growing pattern of shapes. Draw step 1, step 2, step 3 and step 4, so that each step has more shapes than the one before and it grows by the same rule every time. In the note, write your rule and say how many shapes step 10 will have.

rubric.criterion: Draws four steps that grow by a steady rule
Writes a rule that matches the drawing (e.g. 'add one more square on each side', 'add 3 each time')
Gives the correct number for step 10 for their own rule

tasks.guidance: Any regular growth is fine: a line of squares that grows by 1, a tower that grows by 2, triangles made of sticks. Check step 10 against the child's rule (if steps are 2, 4, 6, 8 then step 10 has 20). A repeating pattern (same number every time) is not a growing pattern. Patterns that double are fine if the child states the rule.

tasks.prompt: Step 1: draw a big triangle. Step 2: mark the middle of each side and join the three middle points; this makes a triangle in the middle, which you leave empty, and three corner triangles. Step 3: do the same inside each of the three corner triangles. Draw step 3. In the note, write how many small corner triangles there are at step 2 and at step 3, and how many there will be at step 4.

rubric.criterion: Draws step 3 correctly: the step-2 drawing with each corner triangle split again
Says 3 corner triangles at step 2 and 9 at step 3
Says step 4 will have 27, because each triangle makes 3 new ones (multiply by 3)

tasks.guidance: Counts: 1, 3, 9, 27. Middle points need not be exact if the drawing shows the idea. Some children count every triangle they can see (including the large ones); if their count is clearly explained, mention the difference in feedback but award 'counts' only for 3 and 9 corner triangles. 'Three times as many each time' earns the 'next' point.

tasks.prompt: Fatima has 3 shirts (red, blue and green) and 2 skirts (black and white). She wears one shirt with one skirt. List all the different outfits she can make. Write your list in an organised way, so you can be sure you have not missed any. How many outfits are there?

rubric.criterion: Lists every outfit with no repeats: red-black, red-white, blue-black, blue-white, green-black, green-white
Uses an organised method, e.g. taking each shirt in turn with both skirts, a table or a tree diagram
Says there are 6 outfits, and explains how they know none is missing (e.g. 2 skirts for each of 3 shirts)

tasks.guidance: There are 3 × 2 = 6 outfits. A random list that happens to have all six earns 'list' but not 'order'. A table with shirts down the side and skirts across the top is an excellent organised method. Accept short forms like R-B, R-W.

tasks.prompt: The picture shows a flag standing at the edge of a pond. The flat line is the water. Copy the flag and the water line onto the squared sheet, then draw the flag's reflection in the water, as you would see it upside down in the pond. In the note, say how you found where each corner goes.

rubric.criterion: Copies the flag and the water line
The reflection is upside down below the water line, with the flag still pointing the same way (to the right)
Each corner of the reflection is the same distance below the line as the matching corner is above it
The note explains the method (e.g. counting squares from the water line)

tasks.guidance: In figure units: the pole runs from (3, 4) down to (3, 0); the flag's tip is at (6, 1) and its corners on the pole at (3, 0) and (3, 2). A common mistake is to flip it left-right too, so the flag points left: withhold 'flip'. Another is to draw it the right way up below the water (a slide, not a reflection).

tasks.prompt: Draw an L shape made of 3 squares. Then draw it three more times in a row: each time turned a quarter turn clockwise (like the hand of a clock) from the one before. In the note, say how many quarter turns bring the L back to how it started, and what a half turn does to it.

rubric.criterion: Draws the L after one, two and three quarter turns clockwise, each one correct
Says 4 quarter turns bring it back to the start (a full turn)
Says a half turn (2 quarter turns) turns it upside down, matching their third drawing

tasks.guidance: Award 1 of the 2 'turns' points if one of the three turned shapes is wrong, or if all are turned anticlockwise consistently. A flipped (mirror) L is not a turn; check the short arm's position. Accept 'upside down' for the half turn.

tasks.prompt: Ravi thinks a bag of onions weighs about 2 kg. He has a balance and two 1 kg weights. (1) How can he check his guess? (2) What will he see if the bag is heavier than 2 kg? (3) What will he see if his guess is exactly right?
