tasks.guidance: Learners who write the property for [0, a] only (f(a − x)) and then shift the interval correctly may earn all marks. Answering 3/2 by guessing symmetry without the property earns only 'value'.

tasks.prompt: Evaluate ∫₋₂² (x³ cos x + |x − 1|) dx. For each part of the integrand, name the property of definite integrals you use and say why it applies: show that x³ cos x is an odd function, and split the interval where the expression inside the modulus changes sign.

rubric.criterion: Shows (−x)³ cos(−x) = −x³ cos x, so x³ cos x is odd
Uses ∫₋ₐᵃ g(x) dx = 0 for odd g, with the integral split by linearity
Splits at x = 1: |x − 1| = 1 − x on [−2, 1] and x − 1 on [1, 2]
Evaluates the pieces as 9/2 and 1/2
Total value 5

tasks.guidance: Learners may evaluate ∫|x − 1| as the area of two triangles (9/2 and 1/2); accept this for 'pieces' if the triangles are described. A common error is treating |x − 1| as even on [−2, 2] and doubling ∫₀² — it is not even.

tasks.prompt:
Sketch the parabola y = x² and the line y = 2x + 3 on the same axes, mark their points of intersection, and shade the region enclosed between them. Draw one typical vertical strip in the region.
In the note: show how you found the points of intersection, write the area of the region as a single definite integral (say which graph is on top), and evaluate it.

rubric.criterion: Parabola and line drawn with the intersection points (−1, 1) and (3, 9) marked
Shades only the region between them and draws a vertical strip from the parabola up to the line
Writes the area as ∫₋₁³ [(2x + 3) − x²] dx, with the line on top
Evaluates to 32/3 square units

tasks.guidance: Integrating (x² − (2x + 3)) gives −32/3; a learner who then takes the absolute value without comment loses 'integral' but keeps 'value'. Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt:
The region R is bounded by the parabola y² = x and the line y = x − 2.
(a) Find the points where they meet.
(b) Write the area of R as one integral using horizontal strips.
(c) Explain why vertical strips would need two integrals, and write those two integrals (you need not evaluate them).
(d) Evaluate the area.

rubric.criterion: Points of intersection (1, −1) and (4, 2)
Area = ∫₋₁² [(y + 2) − y²] dy, right boundary minus left boundary
Explains the lower boundary changes at x = 1 and writes ∫₀¹ [√x − (−√x)] dx + ∫₁⁴ [√x − (x − 2)] dx
Area 9/2 square units

tasks.guidance: Accept a sketch in words or a description of which curve is left/right. Learners often use only the upper half of the parabola for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1; that loses 'vertical'.

tasks.prompt:
On the axes, draw the graph of y = 3 for 1 ≤ x ≤ 5 and shade the region between it and the x-axis. Then draw the graph of y = −2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 and shade the region between it and the x-axis.
In the note: (a) explain, using thin vertical strips, why ∫₁⁵ 3 dx is the area of a rectangle, and give its value; (b) find ∫₀³ (−2) dx, and explain why it is not equal to the area of the second shaded region.

rubric.criterion: Both horizontal segments drawn at the right heights and x-ranges, with the rectangles to the x-axis shaded
Explains every strip has height 3 and width dx, so adding them over a width of 4 gives 3 × 4 = 12
The area is 6: the integral counts a region below the x-axis as negative, so area = |integral| here

tasks.guidance: Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt:
A culture of bacteria grows at a rate proportional to the number of bacteria present. At the start there are 500 bacteria, and 4 hours later there are 1500.
(a) Write a differential equation for the number N of bacteria at time t hours, explaining each symbol.
(b) Solve it by separating the variables, and use the data to find every constant.
(c) Verify by substitution that your solution satisfies the differential equation.
(d) Find how long it takes for the culture to reach 13 500 bacteria.

rubric.criterion: dN/dt = kN with k a positive constant (rate proportional to N)
Separates and integrates: ∫ dN/N = ∫ k dt, giving N = 500 e^(kt) using N(0) = 500
Finds k = (ln 3)/4, or writes N = 500 · 3^(t/4)
Differentiates the solution and shows dN/dt = kN
Solves 3^(t/4) = 27 to get t = 12 hours

tasks.guidance: Learners who write ln N = kt + C must turn C into N₀ correctly; e^(kt) + C is a common error that loses 'solve'. Decimal k ≈ 0.2747 is fine if the time comes out as 12 hours (to rounding).

tasks.prompt:
Let a = 3î + ĵ and b = î + 2ĵ (in the xy-plane, so their k̂-components are 0). From the origin O draw OA representing a and OB representing b. Complete the parallelogram OACB, draw the diagonal OC, and draw the vector from B to A.
In the note: (a) explain, using the triangle law, why OC represents a + b, and give a + b in î, ĵ form and its magnitude; (b) explain why the vector from B to A represents a − b, and give it in î, ĵ form; (c) write 2a − b in î, ĵ form.

rubric.criterion: A at (3, 1), B at (1, 2), C at (4, 3), with parallelogram OACB and diagonal OC drawn
Triangle law: OC = OA + AC and AC = OB = b (equal vectors), so a + b = 4î + 3ĵ with |a + b| = 5
BA = BO + OA = −b + a, so a − b = 2î − ĵ

tasks.guidance: Learners who draw the arrow from A to B (b − a) and call it a − b lose 'diff'. Arrowheads must point the right way. Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt:
Points A and B have position vectors a and b relative to an origin O.
(a) Prove that the point P dividing AB internally in the ratio m : n has position vector (mb + na)/(m + n). Describe your figure and name the vector law you use.
(b) State the corresponding result for a point Q dividing AB externally in the ratio m : n (m ≠ n), and explain what changes in the proof.
(c) Use part (a) to show that the centroid of triangle ABC, with vertices at position vectors a, b, c, has position vector (a + b + c)/3.

rubric.criterion: Uses AP : PB = m : n with AP and PB in the same direction to write n·AP = m·PB as vectors
Writes AP = r − a and PB = b − r by the triangle law and solves to r = (mb + na)/(m + n)
External division gives (mb − na)/(m − n), because AQ and QB now point in opposite directions (n·AQ = −m·QB)
Midpoint D of BC has position vector (b + c)/2; dividing AD in the ratio 2 : 1 gives (a + b + c)/3

tasks.guidance: Any correct labelling is fine. The key idea in 'ratio' is turning a ratio of lengths into a vector equation, which needs the same direction; learners who write m·AP = n·PB have the ratio reversed.

tasks.prompt:
(a) Using the dot product, prove that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.
(b) A parallelogram has adjacent sides represented by vectors a and b. Using the cross product, prove that its area is ½|d₁ × d₂|, where d₁ and d₂ are vectors along its diagonals.
(c) A force F = 2î + ĵ − k̂ (newtons) moves a particle in a straight line from the point (1, 1, 2) to the point (3, 2, 1) (coordinates in metres). Find the work done, and explain why the dot product, not the cross product, gives work.

rubric.criterion: (a) Diagonals a + b and a − b; (a + b)·(a − b) = |a|² − |b|² = 0 because |a| = |b|, so the (non-zero) diagonals are perpendicular
(b) Expands (a + b) × (b − a) = 2(a × b), using a × a = b × b = 0 and b × a = −(a × b)
(b) Since the area is |a × b|, concludes area = ½|d₁ × d₂|
(c) Displacement d = 2î + ĵ − k̂ and work F·d = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6 J
(c) Explains work is a scalar: the component of force along the displacement times the distance, which is F·d (a cross product would be a vector, as for torque)

tasks.guidance: Accept diagonals written in either order or sign. In (c), using the position vector of the end point instead of the displacement is the typical error (it gives 7 J); 'work' needs the displacement 2î + ĵ − k̂ and 6 J.

tasks.prompt:
(a) Prove Lagrange's identity: for any vectors a, b, c, d,
(a × b)·(c × d) = (a·c)(b·d) − (a·d)(b·c).
You may use that the dot and cross can be interchanged in a scalar triple product, (u × v)·w = u·(v × w), and the vector triple product formula u × (v × w) = (u·w)v − (u·v)w.
(b) Deduce that |a × b|² = |a|²|b|² − (a·b)², and use it with a·b = |a||b| cos θ to show |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π.

rubric.criterion: Writes (a × b)·(c × d) = a·(b × (c × d)) by interchanging dot and cross
Expands b × (c × d) = (b·d)c − (b·c)d with the formula
Dots with a to reach (a·c)(b·d) − (a·d)(b·c)
(b) Puts c = a and d = b to get |a × b|² = |a|²|b|² − (a·b)²
(b) Gets |a|²|b|²(1 − cos²θ) = |a|²|b|² sin²θ and takes the root using sin θ ≥ 0 on [0, π]

tasks.guidance: Alternative for (a): treat c × d as a single vector w only after expanding (a × b) × ... — any correct use of the two given rules is acceptable. A component-by-component expansion is valid but long; accept it if complete. Not using sin θ ≥ 0 loses 'sine'.

tasks.prompt:
A small workshop in Coimbatore makes school bags and tote bags. The table in the picture shows the cutting time, stitching time and fabric each bag needs, what is available each week, and the profit on each bag. Every bag made is sold.
(a) Formulate a linear programming problem to decide how many of each bag to make each week to maximise profit: name the decision variables (with units), write the objective function and every constraint, including any that come from the situation rather than the table. Do not solve it.
(b) Explain, in the words of this situation, what the feasible region, a feasible solution and the optimal solution are.
(c) Is making 10 school bags and 25 tote bags in a week a feasible plan? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Decision variables x = number of school bags and y = number of tote bags made per week
Maximise Z = 120x + 80y (rupees)
2x + y ≤ 40, x + 2y ≤ 50, 3x + y ≤ 54, and x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (whole numbers)
Explains the feasible region as all weekly plans meeting every limit, a feasible solution as one such plan, and the optimal solution as the feasible plan with the greatest profit
(10, 25) is not feasible: cutting needs 2·10 + 25 = 45 hours > 40

tasks.guidance: Constraints with ≥ instead of ≤ or with the columns swapped (e.g. x + 2y ≤ 40) lose 'constraints'. Non-negativity must be stated; whole-number requirement is a bonus remark, not required.

tasks.prompt:
Minimise Z = 3x + 5y subject to x + 3y ≥ 6, x + y ≥ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Draw the feasible region and mark its corner points.
In the note: give each corner point (showing how you found any corner that is not on an axis), the value of Z at each, and the minimum. The feasible region is unbounded, so explain the extra check needed before you can say the minimum exists, and carry it out. Finally, say whether Z has a maximum on this region.

rubric.criterion: Boundary lines x + 3y = 6 and x + y = 4 drawn, and the unbounded region on the side away from the origin shaded
Corner points (6, 0), (3, 1) and (0, 4), with (3, 1) found by solving the equations
Z = 18, 14, 20 respectively, smallest 14 at (3, 1)
Draws or describes the open half-plane 3x + 5y < 14 and shows it has no point in common with the feasible region, so the minimum is 14 at (3, 1)
Says Z has no maximum, because the region is unbounded and Z grows without limit (e.g. along the x-axis)

tasks.guidance: A learner who stops after the corner table loses 'check' even if the minimum is right: for an unbounded region the half-plane test is what justifies it. Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt:
(a) Explain the difference between mutually exclusive events and independent events, using their definitions in terms of events and probabilities.
(b) For one roll of a fair six-sided die, give an example of two events that are mutually exclusive but not independent, and an example of two events that are independent but not mutually exclusive. Check each claim with probabilities.
(c) Prove that if P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0, then A and B cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.

rubric.criterion: Mutually exclusive: A ∩ B = ∅ (so P(A ∩ B) = 0); independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
A checked example of mutually exclusive, not independent events, e.g. {1} and {2}: P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ 1/36
A checked example of independent, not mutually exclusive events, e.g. 'even' and {1, 2}: P(A ∩ B) = 1/6 = 1/2 · 1/3
Mutually exclusive gives P(A ∩ B) = 0, independence gives P(A)P(B) > 0, a contradiction

tasks.guidance: Independence explained only as 'one does not affect the other' is incomplete for 'defs'; the product rule must appear. Any correct die examples are fine if the probabilities are checked.

tasks.prompt:
A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. Let A be the event 'the card is a king' and B the event 'the card is a heart'.
(a) Decide whether A and B are independent, showing the probabilities you compare.
(b) A classmate says: 'A and B cannot be independent, because the king of hearts is in both.' Explain what is wrong with this reasoning.
(c) Prove that if any two events A and B are independent, then A and B′ (the complement of B) are also independent.

rubric.criterion: P(A) = 1/13, P(B) = 1/4, P(A ∩ B) = 1/52 = P(A)P(B), so A and B are independent
Explains that sharing an outcome only means the events are not mutually exclusive; independence means knowing B does not change the probability of A (P(A | B) = 1/13 = P(A))
(c) Writes A as the disjoint union of A ∩ B and A ∩ B′, so P(A ∩ B′) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B)
(c) Uses independence: P(A) − P(A)P(B) = P(A)(1 − P(B)) = P(A)P(B′)

tasks.guidance: In (c) a Venn diagram is a good aid but the probability steps must be written. Proving only for the cards example earns nothing in (c).

tasks.prompt:
Starting from the graph of y = |x|, sketch y = −2|x − 1| + 3. Draw y = |x| lightly first and label it. On your final graph mark the vertex, the y-intercept and both x-intercepts.
In the note: list, in order, the transformations (translation, reflection, dilation) that take y = |x| to y = −2|x − 1| + 3, giving the direction and size of each; then give the range of the new function.

rubric.criterion: Vertex at (1, 3) with the graph opening downwards
Arms have slopes 2 and −2 (steeper than y = |x|)
y-intercept (0, 1) and x-intercepts (−1/2, 0) and (5/2, 0)
Transformations: translate 1 right, stretch vertically by factor 2, reflect in the x-axis, translate 3 up (stretch and reflection in either order, both before the upward shift)
Range (−∞, 3]

tasks.guidance: Moving the graph 1 to the left (reading x − 1 as 'minus means left') is the typical error; it loses 'vertex' and 'intercepts' only if the points are wrong. In 'order', the upward shift must come after the stretch/reflection; a learner who shifts up 3 first and then reflects gets the wrong graph. Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt: Let a, b and c be real numbers. Prove that the equation (x − a)(x − b) = c² always has real roots, and find exactly when its roots are equal. Then explain, using the graph of y = (x − a)(x − b) and a horizontal line, why this result should be expected.

rubric.criterion: Rewrites as x² − (a + b)x + ab − c² = 0
Computes Δ = (a + b)² − 4(ab − c²) = (a − b)² + 4c²
Concludes Δ ≥ 0 as a sum of squares, so the roots are real
Roots equal exactly when a = b and c = 0 (both squares zero)
Explains y = (x − a)(x − b) is an upward parabola meeting the x-axis at a and b, so its lowest value is ≤ 0, and the line y = c² ≥ 0 must meet it

tasks.guidance: Learners often stop at Δ = a² − 2ab + b² + 4c² without recognising (a − b)²; give 'disc' but not 'real' unless non-negativity is justified.

tasks.prompt:
Sketch y = 2x² − 4x − 6. Mark its x-intercepts, its y-intercept, its vertex and its axis of symmetry.
In the note: explain how you found each of these features, and then use the graph to explain for which real values of k the equation 2x² − 4x − 6 = k has (i) two distinct real roots, (ii) equal roots, (iii) no real roots.

rubric.criterion: x-intercepts (−1, 0) and (3, 0), y-intercept (0, −6)
Vertex (1, −8), axis x = 1, parabola opening upwards
Explains the method: factorising 2(x − 3)(x + 1), x = −b/2a (or completing the square)
Uses horizontal lines y = k: two roots for k > −8, equal roots for k = −8, none for k < −8

tasks.guidance: Accept discriminant reasoning for 'k' if it is linked to the graph (32 + 8k compared with 0). Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt:
In a triangle ABC with the usual notation (a = BC, b = CA, c = AB):
(a) Prove the projection formula a = b cos C + c cos B. Draw the perpendicular from A to the line BC, and treat both the case where B and C are acute and the case where C is obtuse.
(b) Write the other two projection formulas and use all three to derive the cosine rule a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.

rubric.criterion: Acute case: with foot D on BC, BD = c cos B and DC = b cos C, so a = BD + DC
Obtuse C: D lies beyond C, CD = b cos(π − C) = −b cos C, and a = BD − CD gives the same formula
States b = c cos A + a cos C and c = a cos B + b cos A
Multiplies the three formulas by a, b, c respectively and combines them so the cos B and cos C terms cancel
Obtains b² + c² − a² = 2bc cos A, i.e. the cosine rule

tasks.guidance: The right-angled case (C = 90°) is a valid extra but not required. Learners who prove only the acute case lose 'obtuse'. Alternative derivations of the cosine rule (coordinates, Pythagoras) are correct but do not use the projection formulas asked for: award 'cosine' only.

tasks.prompt:
Let a and b be two distinct positive real numbers, and let A, G and H be their arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means.
(a) Write A, G and H in terms of a and b, explaining where the formula for H comes from (a, H, b in harmonic progression means 1/a, 1/H, 1/b are in arithmetic progression).
(b) Prove that G² = AH.
(c) Prove that A > G > H.

rubric.criterion: A = (a + b)/2, G = √(ab), H = 2ab/(a + b), with H derived from 2/H = 1/a + 1/b
Shows AH = ((a + b)/2) · (2ab/(a + b)) = ab = G²
Proves A > G, e.g. from (√a − √b)² > 0, strict because a ≠ b
Deduces G > H, e.g. H = G²/A and A > G > 0 give H < G

tasks.guidance: Learners may prove G > H directly (G − H = √(ab)(√a − √b)²/(a + b) > 0); that is fine. Writing ≥ instead of > without using a ≠ b loses 'ag'.

tasks.prompt: Show that the equation 6x² − xy − 2y² + 3x + 5y − 3 = 0 represents a pair of straight lines. Then find the two lines separately, the point where they meet, and the acute angle between them. Show the condition you test or the factorisation you use.

rubric.criterion: Uses abc + 2fgh − af² − bg² − ch² = 0 with a = 6, h = −1/2, b = −2, g = 3/2, f = 5/2, c = −3 (or a full factorisation) to show it is a pair of lines
Separate lines 2x + y − 1 = 0 and 3x − 2y + 3 = 0
They meet at (−1/7, 9/7)
tan θ = 2√(h² − ab)/|a + b| = 7/4, so the acute angle is tan⁻¹(7/4)

tasks.guidance: Factorising 6x² − xy − 2y² = (2x + y)(3x − 2y) and then matching constants is an equally good method and earns 'condition' if the expansion is checked. The angle can also come from the slopes −2 and 3/2. A common slip is using h = −1 instead of −1/2.

tasks.prompt:
Without expanding the determinant directly, use properties of determinants to prove that
| 1 1 1 |
| a b c |
| a³ b³ c³ | = (a − b)(b − c)(c − a)(a + b + c).
Name the property you use at each step.

rubric.criterion: Applies C₂ → C₂ − C₁ and C₃ → C₃ − C₁ (value unchanged), giving a first row 1, 0, 0
Takes out the common factors (b − a) and (c − a) from the new columns, using b³ − a³ = (b − a)(b² + ab + a²)
Expands along the first row and simplifies (c² + ca + a²) − (b² + ab + a²) = (c − b)(a + b + c)
Rearranges (b − a)(c − a)(c − b)(a + b + c) into (a − b)(b − c)(c − a)(a + b + c) with correct signs

tasks.guidance: Accept the factor-theorem argument: a = b gives two equal columns so (a − b) is a factor, similarly (b − c), (c − a); then a degree-4 symmetric argument gives the factor k(a + b + c) and k = 1 by comparing a coefficient. That earns all criteria if the coefficient comparison is shown.

rubric.criterion: (a) Takes determinants: |A| |adj A| = | |A| Iₙ | = |A|ⁿ, using |kIₙ| = kⁿ
(a) Divides by |A| ≠ 0 to get |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹
(b) Divides the identity by |A| to show (1/|A|) adj A is a two-sided inverse; if |A| = 0 no inverse exists (and the division is impossible)
(c) Applies the identity to adj A (non-singular by (a)): (adj A) adj(adj A) = |A|ⁿ⁻¹ Iₙ
(c) Multiplies on the left by A and uses A adj A = |A| Iₙ to get adj(adj A) = |A|ⁿ⁻² A

tasks.guidance: Checking (a) for one 2 × 2 or 3 × 3 matrix is not a proof. In (b), for 'must be non-singular' accept either reason: the formula divides by |A|, or AA⁻¹ = I gives |A||A⁻¹| = 1, which forces |A| ≠ 0.

tasks.prompt:
For each function, decide whether it is continuous at the given point. Justify with the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the function value, and if it is discontinuous, classify the discontinuity as removable, jump or infinite, explaining your choice.
(a) f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, f(2) = 3, at x = 2.
(b) g(x) = [x] (greatest integer function) at x = 1.
(c) h(x) = 1/x² for x ≠ 0, h(0) = 0, at x = 0.
(d) Say how to redefine f(2) so that f becomes continuous at 2, and explain why no choice of g(1) makes g continuous at 1.

rubric.criterion: (a) Both one-sided limits are 4 but f(2) = 3, so a removable discontinuity
(b) Left-hand limit 0, right-hand limit 1 (= g(1)): a jump discontinuity
(c) Both one-sided limits are +∞, so an infinite discontinuity
(d) Redefine f(2) = 4; for g the one-sided limits differ, so the limit does not exist and no value of g(1) helps

tasks.guidance: Learners who cancel (x − 2) must note x ≠ 2. In (b), the commonest error is LHL = 1. Accept 'discontinuity of the second kind' for (c) if the infinite limits are stated.

tasks.prompt: Let y = log(x + √(x² + 1)) (natural logarithm). Prove that (x² + 1) d²y/dx² + x dy/dx = 0. Show each derivative and name the rule used.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates with the chain rule: dy/dx = (1 + x/√(x² + 1))/(x + √(x² + 1))
Simplifies dy/dx to 1/√(x² + 1)
Finds d²y/dx² = −x/(x² + 1)^(3/2), or differentiates √(x² + 1) · dy/dx = 1 implicitly
Substitutes to show (x² + 1) d²y/dx² + x dy/dx = 0

tasks.guidance: The implicit route (square, differentiate, cancel) is equally good and earns 'second' and 'relation'. A sign error in d²y/dx² is common.

tasks.prompt:
Let S = {z ∈ ℂ : |z − 2 − i| ≤ 2 and |z| ≤ |z − 4|}. On the Argand plane draw the boundary of each condition and shade S.
In the note: write z = x + iy and turn each condition into an equation or inequality in x and y; describe each boundary in words (centre and radius, or which perpendicular bisector); and say whether the boundary points belong to S.

rubric.criterion: (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² ≤ 4: circle with centre (2, 1) and radius 2 drawn
|z| ≤ |z − 4| becomes x ≤ 2; the line x = 2 is the perpendicular bisector of the points 0 and 4
Shades only the left half of the disc (x ≤ 2)
Boundaries drawn solid and stated to be included, because both conditions use ≤

tasks.guidance: Learners often put the centre at (−2, −1) (sign error) or shade the right half. Squaring |z| ≤ |z − 4| is valid because both sides are non-negative. Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt:
Use de Moivre's theorem to find the three cube roots of 8i, giving each in the form a + ib. Plot the three roots on the Argand plane and join them.
In the note: write 8i in polar form, show the general formula you use with k = 0, 1, 2, and explain why the three roots lie on one circle and form an equilateral triangle.

rubric.criterion: 8i = 8(cos π/2 + i sin π/2)
Plots the three points on the circle of radius 2 about the origin, at (±√3, 1) and (0, −2)
Explains all three have modulus 2 (one circle) and their arguments differ by 2π/3, so the chords joining them are equal

tasks.guidance: Learners who forget the 2kπ get only one root; that loses 'formula' and 'roots'. Arguments in degrees (30°, 150°, 270°) are acceptable in the working. Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt:
(a) State Lagrange's mean value theorem, including all its hypotheses.
(b) Use it to prove that x/(1 + x) < log(1 + x) < x for every x > 0 (natural logarithm). Check that each hypothesis holds for the function and interval you choose.

rubric.criterion: If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there is c ∈ (a, b) with f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)
Chooses f(t) = log(1 + t) on [0, x] and checks continuity and differentiability (1 + t > 0 there)
Obtains log(1 + x)/x = 1/(1 + c) for some c with 0 < c < x
Uses 0 < c < x to get 1/(1 + x) < 1/(1 + c) < 1 (strict) and multiplies by x > 0 to reach the result

tasks.guidance: A proof through monotonic functions (g(x) = x − log(1 + x) increasing, etc.) is correct mathematics but does not use the theorem the task asks for: award 'statement' only and say so in feedback. Stating the theorem with 'closed' and 'open' intervals swapped loses 'statement'.

tasks.prompt:
Sketch the curve y = x²/(x − 1). Find and show on your sketch: the domain, the intercepts, the vertical asymptote, the oblique (slant) asymptote, the local maximum and local minimum, and where the curve is concave up or concave down. Draw the asymptotes as dashed lines.
In the note: show how you found the oblique asymptote, give f′(x) and f″(x), and explain why the curve has no point of inflection even though its concavity changes.

rubric.criterion: Vertical asymptote x = 1 and oblique asymptote y = x + 1 (from x²/(x − 1) = x + 1 + 1/(x − 1)), drawn dashed
f′(x) = x(x − 2)/(x − 1)²: local maximum (0, 0), local minimum (2, 4)
f″(x) = 2/(x − 1)³: concave down on (−∞, 1), concave up on (1, ∞); no inflection point because x = 1 is not in the domain
Left branch lies below y = x + 1 and falls to −∞ as x → 1⁻; right branch lies above and rises to +∞ as x → 1⁺
Domain ℝ ∖ {1}, and the only intercept is the origin

tasks.guidance: Learners often find the oblique asymptote as y = x (dividing incorrectly) or claim an inflection at x = 1. Mark the drawing together with the note: a feature counts when it is drawn or stated in the note and is in the right place; a freehand sketch is judged on its key features, not on pixel accuracy.

tasks.prompt:
Let f(x, y) = x³ log(y/x) for x > 0, y > 0 (natural logarithm).
(a) Find ∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, ∂²f/∂y∂x and ∂²f/∂x∂y, and verify that the two mixed partial derivatives are equal.
(b) Show directly from the definition that f is homogeneous, and state its degree.
(c) Verify Euler's theorem for f.

rubric.criterion: ∂f/∂x = 3x² log(y/x) − x² and ∂f/∂y = x³/y
Both mixed partial derivatives equal 3x²/y
f(tx, ty) = t³x³ log(y/x) = t³ f(x, y) for t > 0, so f is homogeneous of degree 3
x ∂f/∂x + y ∂f/∂y = 3x³ log(y/x) − x³ + x³ = 3f

tasks.guidance: Learners may write log(y/x) = log y − log x before differentiating; that is fine. Missing the −x² term in ∂f/∂x (from differentiating −log x) is the typical slip, which then breaks 'euler'.

tasks.prompt:
Define a * b = a + b − 3ab.
(a) Prove that * is a binary operation on ℤ, and show that it is not a binary operation on ℕ.
(b) Prove that * is commutative and associative on ℤ.
(c) Find the identity element of (ℤ, *), and decide which integers have an inverse in ℤ under *, with reasons.

rubric.criterion: Closure on ℤ: sums and products of integers are integers
Counterexample on ℕ, e.g. 1 * 1 = −1 ∉ ℕ
a * b = b * a because addition and multiplication of integers are commutative
Both (a * b) * c and a * (b * c) expand to a + b + c − 3(ab + bc + ca) + 9abc
Identity 0, checked: a * 0 = 0 * a = a
Solving a * b = 0 gives b = a/(3a − 1); only a = 0 has an integer inverse, because 0 < |a| < |3a − 1| for every non-zero integer a

tasks.guidance: For 'inverse', checking a few values is not enough; the learner needs a general reason why a/(3a − 1) is not an integer for a ≠ 0 (any valid argument).

tasks.prompt:
(a) Use a truth table to show that (p → q) ↔ (¬q → ¬p) is a tautology.
(b) Classify (p ∧ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ q) as a tautology, a contradiction or a contingency, and justify your answer.
(c) Write the dual of (p ∧ T) ∨ (q ∧ ¬r), where T is the statement that is always true.
(d) Without a truth table, using known laws (name each), prove that ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q.

rubric.criterion: (a) A four-row table with correct columns for p → q, ¬q → ¬p and the biconditional, whose final column is all T
(b) A contradiction: e.g. ¬p ∨ q ≡ ¬(p ∧ ¬q) by De Morgan, so it has the form X ∧ ¬X (or a table with every row F)
(d) p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q; De Morgan gives ¬¬p ∧ ¬q; double negation gives p ∧ ¬q, each law named

tasks.guidance: In (c), learners often forget to change T to F, or negate the variables (the dual does not negate them). In (d), any correct named chain of laws is acceptable.
